name: The Metamorphosis
blurb: Kafka's novella of a salesman who wakes up transformed into a giant insect
title: The Metamorphosis Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: The Metamorphosis summary: Gregor Samsa, Grete and the family, what happens in each of the three parts, and what Kafka's ending means.
h1: The Metamorphosis: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: The Metamorphosis (Die Verwandlung) is a novella by the Prague-born German-language writer Franz Kafka, written in 1912 and published in 1915. Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman who supports his parents and sister, wakes up one morning to find he has turned into a huge insect-like creature. The story never explains the transformation. Instead it follows, in three parts, how Gregor and his family deal with it inside their apartment.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: A traveling salesman whose wages pay his family's bills and his father's debts
Gregor's teenage younger sister, who plays the violin
Gregor's father, whose business failed five years earlier
Gregor's mother, who suffers from asthma
An elderly widow hired to do the heavy cleaning
Bearded men who rent a room in the apartment

body: Part I: Gregor wakes in his room to find himself a giant vermin, lying on a hard, armored back with many thin legs waving. His first worry is not his body but his job: he has overslept and missed his train. He reflects on how much he hates his exhausting work and stays only to pay off the debt his parents owe his boss. His family knocks at the door, and then the chief clerk arrives from the firm to ask why he is late, hinting that his position is in doubt. Gregor's voice has become an unintelligible squeak. After a long struggle he turns the key with his jaws and opens the door. The clerk flees in horror, his mother collapses, and his father, hissing and waving a cane and a newspaper, drives him back into his room, where he is injured squeezing through the doorway.

Part II: Grete takes charge of feeding him and learns that he now prefers rotting food to fresh milk. Gregor hides under the sofa so she will not have to see him. He overhears that his father has kept some savings he never mentioned, and he had secretly planned to pay for Grete to study the violin at the conservatory. The family begins to take jobs. Gregor starts to crawl over the walls and ceiling, so Grete and the mother decide to clear out his furniture. Gregor, wanting to keep some trace of his human life, clings to a framed picture of a woman in furs; his mother sees him and faints. When his father comes home he chases Gregor and pelts him with apples. One lodges in Gregor's back and stays there, rotting, and the wound cripples him.

Part III: Over the following month the family grows tired and resentful. They take in three lodgers to make money and rely on a charwoman for the heavy work, and Grete's care becomes careless; Gregor's room fills with dust and junk. One evening Grete plays the violin for the lodgers. Gregor, moved by the music, creeps out into the living room. The lodgers see him, announce that they are leaving and refuse to pay. Grete then tells her parents that the creature must go: if it were really Gregor, she says, he would have left them of his own accord. Gregor drags himself back into his room, thinks of his family with love, and dies before dawn.

In the morning the charwoman finds his dried-up body and tells the family it has been disposed of. Mr. Samsa orders the lodgers out of the apartment. The three surviving Samsas take the day off, write notes to their employers and ride a tram into the countryside. On the way they realize that their jobs are actually promising, and that a smaller, cheaper apartment would suit them better. The parents notice that Grete has grown into a lovely young woman and think it will soon be time to find her a husband. In the last image she stands up and stretches her young body.

The ending is deliberately cold: Gregor's death brings relief, not grief, and the story continues happily without him. Kafka gave no single explanation, and readings are debated. The most common ones:

ul: The real metamorphosis is the family's: once the breadwinner can no longer earn, they become independent, and Grete in particular turns from a child into an adult who replaces him.
Alienation and work: Gregor was already treated as a tool for earning money, and the transformation makes that visible; once he is useless he is discarded.
A biographical reading: critics often connect the story to Kafka's difficult relationship with his domineering father, described in his Letter to His Father.

body: Other critics read the insect as illness or disability, and the family's response as the way a household can come to see a dependent relative as a burden.

ul: Alienation: Gregor is cut off from his family long before the transformation, and afterward he cannot even speak to them.
Duty and money: the family's love for Gregor seems tied to his wages, and they recover once they earn for themselves.
Identity: Gregor's mind stays human while his body and habits change, raising the question of what makes him still himself.
Family and sacrifice: Gregor gives up his own life to support others and finally accepts that they want him gone.
The absurd: an impossible event is reported in plain, matter-of-fact language, and no one asks why it happened.
Length: a novella of about 70 pages in three parts; it can be read in one or two sittings.
Original language: German. The first sentence's word for the creature, Ungeziefer, means vermin rather than a specific insect, so translations vary between insect, bug, cockroach and vermin.
Kafka asked his publisher that the creature itself not be drawn on the first edition's cover.
What teachers usually ask about: why the transformation is never explained, how Grete changes, and how the ending reflects on the family.

check.q: What injures Gregor badly in Part II?
options: An apple his father throws that lodges in his back
check.why: His father pelts him with apples, and one stays lodged in his back and rots there.

check.q: Who first says the family must get rid of the creature?
check.why: After the lodgers leave, Grete tells her parents that the creature is no longer Gregor and must go.

check.q: What does the family do after Gregor dies?
options: They take a tram trip to the countryside
They move to the city center
check.why: They take the day off, ride a tram into the country and make hopeful plans.

faq.q: What kind of insect does Gregor turn into?
faq.a: Kafka never specifies. The German word Ungeziefer means vermin, and the text describes an armored back, a segmented belly and many thin legs; the charwoman calls him a dung beetle.
Weakened by the rotting apple wound and by not eating, and knowing his family wants him gone, he dies alone in his room before dawn.

faq.q: Why does Gregor turn into a bug?
faq.a: The story never says. Kafka treats the transformation as a given, and the focus is on how Gregor and his family respond to it.
